target_identification.speaker: Jane
target_identification.anchor_quote:
There is no dishonour, no breach of promise, no desertion in the case.
I am not under the slightest obligation to go to India, especially with
strangers. With you I would have ventured much, because I admire,
confide in, and, as a sister, I love you; but I am convinced that, go
when and with whom I would, I should not live long in that climate.

T.reason: Jane directly avows love for St John and explicitly characterizes it as sisterly. It is a deliberate presentation of her affectionate mental state, irrespective of whether St John welcomes or reciprocates it.

evidence.quotation:
because I admire,
confide in, and, as a sister, I love you

P.reason: The avowal does not itself create, renew, or invoke an obligation. Jane uses her sisterly affection and trust to explain why she had been willing to venture abroad with St John, while expressly denying that she promised or remains obligated to go. Her offer to serve as his assistant is a separate, disputed proposal rather than undertaking force carried by “I love you.”

O.reason: Beyond avowing affection, the expression reassures St John of Jane’s regard while drawing a relational boundary: her love is sisterly, not marital. It also helps explain why she trusted him enough to contemplate danger, without conceding his allegation that she was bound by a promise.

original_speech_situation: Jane and St John are disputing whether she has promised or engaged herself to missionary work in India. St John treats her earlier willingness as binding and has rejected accompanying her unless she becomes his wife. Jane denies any obligation, distinguishes her willingness to accompany this trusted, admired man from going with strangers, avows sisterly love, and then explains that she fears the climate would kill her and that she may have reasons to remain in England.
undertaking_and_uptake: The focal expression undertakes nothing. Jane had separately offered to accompany St John as his assistant or sister, but she now explicitly denies that this amounted to a formal promise or obligation. St John disputes her position and frames withdrawal as dishonour, so there is no shared uptake of a binding undertaking. He also does not treat the avowal as acceptance of his marriage proposal; the immediately following exchange instead turns to her fear and her attachment to Mr Rochester.
recognition_note: The supplied passages are recognisable as Charlotte Brontë’s Jane Eyre.
limitations: The supplied first-person narration strongly supports genuine sisterly friendship and the absence of romantic love for St John, but sincerity remains literary evidence rather than independently verifiable fact. The later conclusion concerns subsequent relationships and does not convert this focal avowal into a promise.
